claims.text: Integrating high-throughput experimentation with machine-learning-guided thermomechanical processing can create engineered hierarchical microstructures in high-entropy alloys.
Conventional HEAs generally exhibit simple microstructures and trade-offs between mechanical properties.
Systematically varying cooling rates, annealing temperatures, deformation schedules, and composition can induce heterogeneous hierarchical microstructures.
Machine-learning models can correlate processing conditions with mechanical performance and iteratively refine the processing protocol.
The approach is effective when phase segregation is minimized and the desired microstructural features remain stable.
A hierarchical HEA microstructure can comprise nanoscale strengthening precipitates embedded in a ductile matrix.
A hierarchical HEA microstructure can comprise alternating lamellar or duplex phases.
Hierarchical lamellar or duplex microstructures can concurrently activate strengthening and crack-arresting mechanisms.
Combining nanoscale precipitate strengthening with ductile matrix regions reduces the usual strength–ductility trade-off.
Composite or lamellar architectures improve load distribution.
Composite lamellar architectures provide crack-arresting capability.
The proposed hierarchical architectures increase Young's modulus.
The proposed hierarchical architectures increase fracture resistance.
The optimized HEAs will exhibit simultaneous statistically significant improvements in strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture toughness.
Each of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture toughness is expected to improve by more than 15% relative to the conventional control.
Traditional casting or standard thermomechanical processing typically optimizes one HEA property at the expense of others.
The hypothesis should hold in HEA systems having processing windows that permit stable phase formation.
The hypothesis may fail in alloys prone to severe segregation.
The hypothesis may fail when the induced heterostructure degrades under high-temperature or extreme loading conditions.

Failure of the optimized samples to achieve a statistically significant improvement exceeding 15% in all four targeted properties relative to composition-matched controls would falsify the hypothesis.
